rainbow-creek.story:
The Independent State of Rainbow Creek was a farm at Cowwarr, on the Thomson River in Victoria, Australia, that seceded from the state of Victoria over flooding. The name comes from a channel the river cut by itself. In the 1930s a road bridge was built too close to the flood line. In a violent flood in 1952 debris jammed against it, and the river carved a new course around it, straight through private farms. This was Rainbow Creek.

Later floods widened it, and a weir built in 1954 sent more water into it. By the late 1970s it was 8 metres deep and over 50 metres wide. The farmers were caught in the rules. They paid the council for land now under water, because their deeds did not show the creek. They paid the state water commission for using the creek's water for irrigation, and they paid a third levy to a trust meant to stop the erosion, which went on regardless. They built their own bridges, and severe floods in 1978 washed those away with crops, stock and equipment.

Thomas Barnes, a retired British and Victorian police officer who had owned the Yammacoona property below the weir since 1970, led the farmers. When they were refused compensation in 1978, Barnes and about thirty others signed a declaration of war on Victoria on 19 December 1978 and served it on the state governor before television cameras on 16 January 1979. They rejected a government offer of loans. On 23 July 1979 Barnes declared Yammacoona seceded from Victoria, named himself Governor and swore allegiance to Queen Elizabeth II, in imitation of Hutt River, a farm in Western Australia that had declared itself independent in 1970.

Barnes issued passports, stamps and banknotes to publicise the farmers' cause. Barnes retired to Queensland in the mid-1980s because of ill health, and the flooding dispute was never resolved. The law governing the farm did not change.
rainbow-creek.why: 'The state issued passports' read as Victoria; Barnes issued them. Added exact dates of the declaration of war.

republic-of-lakotah.story:
The Republic of Lakotah was a proposed independent country for the Lakota, a Native American people often grouped under the name Sioux. Its claimed land covered about 200,000 square kilometres of the northern Great Plains in the United States, in parts of North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Wyoming and Montana. That land now holds Indian reservations and non-Native towns alike.

The background is a set of treaties. In the 1800s the United States signed treaties with the Lakota as it would with a foreign power, and the 1851 Treaty of Fort Laramie set out a large Lakota territory. The proposed borders copied that treaty: the Yellowstone River to the north, the North Platte to the south, the Missouri to the east and an irregular line to the west. A later dispute is central to Lakota grievances. The United States took the Black Hills of South Dakota for gold mining after the collapse of the 1868 Fort Laramie treaty. In 1980, in United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians, the Supreme Court awarded eight Sioux tribes $105 million as compensation but gave back no land. The tribal governments have refused the money.

On 17 December 2007 four activists calling themselves the Lakota Freedom Delegation went to Washington, D.C., and contacted the State Department. Their leader was Russell Means, a prominent member of the American Indian Movement since the late 1960s, who called himself chief facilitator of a provisional government. The others were Garry Rowland, Duane Martin and Phyllis Young. Their statement said the Lakota were withdrawing from the treaties, citing the colonial apartheid of the reservation system, along with unemployment, poverty, disease and repeated treaty violations. It invited the United States to negotiate and warned that otherwise Lakotah would file liens, which are legal claims against property, on real estate deals across the five states.

The plan on paper was a loose confederation. Citizenship would be open to any resident of any race, with its own passports and driving licences, no nationwide taxes, and local taxes only with the consent of those taxed. The provisional capital was to be Porcupine, South Dakota. In January 2008 the group suggested that independence could follow a Compact of Free Association, the arrangement the United States has with Palau, Micronesia and the Marshall Islands.

The main weakness was support among the Lakota themselves. The delegation dismissed the elected tribal governments as "stay-by-the-fort Indians", and those governments had not been consulted. The Rosebud Sioux and Cheyenne River chairmen said publicly that they did not back it. A treaty has two sides, and one side can announce that it is leaving, but the other side does not have to answer. The State Department referred questions elsewhere, and a Bureau of Indian Affairs official said the withdrawal did not mean anything.

In 2008 the group filed liens on federal land in a South Dakota county, and these were rejected. It asked embassies for recognition without success. Means ran for president of the Pine Ridge Reservation that year, treating the vote as a test of support, and lost 2,277 to 1,918. Means died in Rapid City, South Dakota, on 22 October 2012. In 2020 the scholar Hiroshi Fukurai wrote that the United States, the United Nations and its members had largely ignored the 2007 declaration. The claim was never tested in a court. The claim rested on real treaties with a named people, and it still lacked backing from the Lakota's own governments and any response from the United States.

add_sources.t: Russell Means

republic-of-lakotah.why: Added missing outcome: Means's death in 2012 and the later scholarly assessment.

sovereign-yidindji-government.story:
The Sovereign Yidindji Government is a government set up by members of the Yidindji, an Aboriginal people of northern Queensland in Australia, who renounced their legal ties with Australia in 2014 (a list of micronations says 2013). Aboriginal peoples lived on the continent long before Britain claimed it, and some argue that their sovereignty, the right to rule themselves, was never given up. The Yidindji government is an attempt to act on that argument.

Gudju Gudju Gimuybara is chief minister and Murrumu Walubara Yidindji is foreign and trade minister. The claimed area covers about 2,500 square kilometres south of Port Douglas, through the city of Cairns and inland across the Atherton Tablelands, plus 80 kilometres of sea.

It issues its own driver's licences and number plates. This is where the claim met the state. In May 2015 Queensland police charged Murrumu, a former television journalist then known as Jeremy Geia, after finding him with a licence and plates from the Yidindji government, and he argued that the police had no jurisdiction, or legal authority, over him. In August 2015 he was arrested on a warrant and brought before Cairns Magistrates Court, where for two days he repeated that he was "Murrumu in the appropriate persona", and he was arrested again in the dock. Magistrate Robert Spencer then released him, saying that a notice to appear would be sent to Mr Geia and that the matter would be heard without him if he did not come. How the traffic case finally ended is not known.

An earlier charge did reach an end. In January 2015 he had been arrested in Canberra for trespass after refusing to leave a public housing property in Kambah that he was setting up as a Yidindji embassy, and he spent three nights in custody. Magistrate Bernadette Boss of the Australian Capital Territory dismissed the charge for insufficient evidence.

In 2022 the group launched a digital Sovereign Yidindji Dollar, pegged to the Australian dollar and said to be backed by gold and silver. It hopes for a memorandum of understanding, a formal written agreement, with the Australian government, and it has approached Russia and Venezuela about diplomatic relations. No such agreement or recognition is known. The case differs from a joke country because its founders belong to a people with a claim that predates the state.

add_sources.t: SBS NITV, Freed Murrumu to thank magistrate
Canberra Times, Trespass case dismissed
Vice News, An Indigenous activist was arrested

sovereign-yidindji-government.why: 'How the case ended is not known' was too broad: added the August 2015 court events and the dismissed Canberra trespass charge. The final result of the traffic case is still not found.

sunda-empire.story:
The Sunda Democratic Empire was an invented empire based in or near Bandung, on the Indonesian island of Java, claiming to succeed the empire of Alexander the Great and to have authority over all countries. It had no link to the Sundanese, the local people of West Java, according to its own spokesman. Its history runs through a money scam, an immigration case and a viral video.

Around 2003 Nasri Banks learned of the empire from unnamed sources, and his wife Raden Ratna Ningrum said it descended from Alexander. That year a man named Jhonson Low showed Nasri a certificate for a deposit of 2 billion dollars at an offshore bank, and the couple gave him money to recover it. Their daughter Fathia later received a paper for 500 million dollars addressed to her as a princess. Believing the story, she and her sister Lamira set off to research the empire.

In July 2007 Malaysia detained the sisters for trying to enter Sarawak from Brunei on Sunda Empire diplomatic passports. A court freed them in January 2008, but they went on claiming Sunda Empire citizenship and refused to accept Indonesian citizenship. That left Malaysia with nowhere to deport them, so the authorities treated them as stateless, meaning belonging to no country, and held them at an immigration depot under the supervision of the UN refugee agency.

The group was active from 2017. In early 2020 a video spread online showing Rangga Sasana, calling himself secretary general, addressing people in military-style uniforms and blue berets. He invited all countries to register with the empire, which he said would settle their debts to the World Bank. Indonesian Wikipedia articles on the United Nations and NATO were altered to mention it. Police arrested the leaders for fraud that January.

At trial in June 2020, Nasri said the declaration was an attempt to have his daughters sent home. Indonesian courts did not need to rule on the history of the empire. On 27 October 2020 all three were sentenced to two years in prison under ordinary law, for spreading false information and disturbing the peace, and they were freed in 2021 under a pandemic release policy. Rangga Sasana became a minor internet personality and died in December 2022. Scholars have worried that such invented kingdoms, which appeared at about the same time elsewhere in Java, could use romantic tales of ancient rulers to deceive people.

vitalia.story:
Vitalia was a temporary village focused on longevity, the science of living longer, held in the first months of 2024 in Próspera. Próspera is a privately run zone on the Honduran island of Roatán, set up under a Honduran law that allowed such zones their own legal rules. Longevity advocates at the earlier Zuzalu gathering had made a new jurisdiction and rules for longevity science a main topic, and Próspera offered a place with separate rules.

The village had a laboratory for biohacking, meaning self-experiment to improve the body, along with workout groups and a biomedical hackathon, a contest to build projects quickly. It is listed as a spin-off of Zuzalu, an earlier pop-up village in Montenegro. Its organisers hoped it would lead to a permanent home base. A later pop-up in Próspera focused on longevity and biotechnology, Infinita City, ran from 6 January to 3 March 2025 and says it is seeding a permanent biotech district there.

The village ended after its 2024 session, although events under the name Vitalia Forever were advertised for 2025. Vitalia made no claim of its own to govern land. Its legal footing was borrowed from Próspera, so its standing depended on how Honduras treats that zone. In April 2022 the Honduran Congress repealed the laws that created such zones, while existing zones were to continue for 50 years. In September 2024 the Honduran Supreme Court declared the zones unconstitutional. Próspera has threatened Honduras with a claim of about 11 billion dollars if its development is halted. How many people attended, what it cost and what its experiments found are not known.
vitalia.mechanism: Vitalia used a zone with its own legal rules to host experiments, so its standing depends on how Honduras treats Próspera, a type of zone the Honduran Supreme Court declared unconstitutional in September 2024. The village made no claim of its own to govern land.

add_sources.t: Zone for Employment and Economic Development
Infinita City, Roatán 2025
LongBio 2024 at Vitalia, 19-21 January
Vitalia Forever 2025

vitalia.why: Vitalia was running in January 2024, not only February. Added the 2022 repeal, the September 2024 Supreme Court ruling and the later Infinita City pop-up.

zad-notre-dame-des-landes.story:
The ZAD of Notre-Dame-des-Landes was a long occupation of a mostly farming area of 1,650 hectares near Nantes in western France, set up to stop a planned airport. ZAD stands for zone à défendre, or Zone to Defend, a play on the official planning term for a development zone. People there ran their own daily life for years on land the state had set aside for a project.

The state had planned an airport there since the 1960s, and local farmers and environmental groups opposed it for decades. As residents were told to leave, some refused and became squatters, and activists joined them, building homes and living in the trees. The first occupation was the Rosiers farm in August 2007. In 2012 the prime minister, Jean-Marc Ayrault, a former mayor of Nantes, said the airport would happen.

In October 2012 the state began an eviction called Operation Caesar, with 2,000 police. Occupiers used barricades, human chains and farmers' tractors. After police destroyed 13 cabins and farmhouses, over 40,000 people marched on 17 November and built a new hamlet by hand, with a bar, kitchen, workshops, dormitories, first aid post and pirate radio, guarded by 40 linked tractors. More than 200 support committees formed across France, and the government backed down.

Daily life grew more settled. By 2017 there were around 70 networked sites, with vegetable plots, a bakery using local grain, a brewery, a pirate radio station, a newspaper and herds of cows, goats and sheep. Decisions were made through shared structures and debate among the occupiers.

On 17 January 2018 Prime Minister Edouard Philippe announced that the airport would be dropped and the existing Nantes airport redeveloped, and said the squatters had until spring to leave. The victory split the occupiers. Some wanted to negotiate with the state, and others wanted to stay fully outside it. In April 2018 the state sent in police, and over 10 days they fired 11,000 tear gas canisters and stun grenades. Squatters reported 272 injuries and police 77. The state estimated that 29 projects had been destroyed and 60 to 70 remained.

Philippe halted the operation on 26 April while the occupiers' representatives sought legal recognition for 28 projects. Fifteen were accepted, including a sheep farm making wool and a buckwheat pancake business, and evictions of other sites resumed in May. That month a 21-year-old man had his right hand amputated after an injury from a police canister. In April 2019 occupiers were still hoping to sign leases, and twenty projects opened to visitors. In 2020 about 200 people lived on the site, the prefect described relations with the state as relaxed but without full mutual understanding, and the construction group Vinci was still pressing the state for 1 billion euros in damages. The occupiers had stopped the airport, after a campaign of about 50 years, and those who stayed did so under permission from the state, through ordinary French land and farm law.
zad-notre-dame-des-landes.why: Added later outcomes through 2020 and the most serious reported injury.

project-hyperion.story:
Project Hyperion studies generation ships, meaning crewed ships whose voyage to another star would last longer than a human life. People would be born, live and die on board, and only their descendants would arrive. The researcher Andreas Hein started the project in December 2011 from WARR, a student group at the Technical University of Munich in Germany, as part of the Icarus Interstellar program. Its stated aim is to assess whether crewed interstellar flight could be done with current and near-future technology, and it has led to some of the most detailed designs of such ships so far.

The team published a study in the Journal of the British Interplanetary Society in 2012, including an assessment of world ship designs and of the population needed. In 2014 the researcher Cameron Smith used its data to estimate how large a population must be to stay genetically healthy over the trip. Core members later moved to a similar project at the Initiative for Interstellar Studies and presented results at a European Space Agency workshop in 2019.

A design competition opened in November 2024. Its rules set a voyage of 250 years for 1,000 people, give or take 500, to a rocky planet whose ecosystem had been prepared by an earlier probe. Teams also had to design how the society aboard would be organised, including how roles are allocated and enforced and how conflict and unethical behaviour are handled. Results came in July 2025. First place went to the Italian team Chrysalis, second to WFP Extreme of Poland and third to Systema Stellare Proximum of Malaysia.

The rules name no particular star or planet, and the project remains a paper study. The competition treated government as an internal design question, and the law outside the ship would still reach it. Under Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the country that registered the ship keeps legal authority over it and its crew, with no end distance stated. Under Article VI that country must also supervise any private group that launches. So a generation ship would leave Earth as some country's legal responsibility, and the children aboard would be bound by rules set before their birth.

add_sources.t: Space.com, Project Hyperion competition

project-hyperion.why: Text said nothing is reported on governance or destination. The competition rules set a destination type, a population and a requirement to design social organisation.

assange-ecuador-embassy.story:
Julian Assange, the Australian co-founder of the leaks website WikiLeaks, lived for nearly seven years inside Ecuador's embassy in London. The embassy is a suite of rooms on part of the ground floor of a block of flats at 3 Hans Crescent, near the Harrods store, in a building that also holds the Colombian embassy and private apartments.

People often think of an embassy as foreign soil, and it is not. The land stays part of the host country. Under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, the treaty on how countries treat each other's diplomats, embassy premises are protected, so the host country's officials may not enter without the permission of the head of the mission. That rule gives a person inside protection from arrest for as long as the embassy lets them stay and no longer.

Sweden wanted to question Assange over four alleged sexual offences. After Britain's Supreme Court dismissed his appeal against being sent there, he breached his bail and entered the embassy on 19 June 2012. Ecuador granted him diplomatic asylum on 16 August. Britain did not accept this, so he could not leave. Police notes photographed outside said he was to be arrested under all circumstances if he came out.

Britain suggested it could use a 1987 British law, the Diplomatic and Consular Premises Act, to enter and arrest him after giving notice, then withdrew the suggestion after Ecuador called this a clear breach of international law. Police instead guarded the building, at a reported cost of £6.5 million in the first two years. By February 2015 the cost had reached £10 million, and Scotland Yard ended its round-the-clock guard on 12 October 2015. He spoke to supporters from a low balcony in August 2012, and Ecuador paid a security company for over five years to monitor his visitors, as the Guardian revealed in 2018.

Swedish prosecutors dropped their investigation in May 2017. In April 2019 President Lenín Moreno accused Assange of repeatedly violating the terms of his asylum and ended it, and on 11 April British police, invited in by Ecuador, arrested him. Sweden reopened its rape investigation in May 2019 and dropped it again on 19 November 2019. He was held in Belmarsh prison until June 2024. On 26 June 2024, in the Northern Mariana Islands, he pleaded guilty to one US count of conspiring to obtain and publish national defence information. His sentence of five years and two months was counted as already served in Britain, and he was freed that day.

An embassy kept British police out for seven years, but only on terms set by Ecuador's government. When that government withdrew its permission, the protection ended the same day, and Assange had no way to stop it.

add_sources.t: Dawn, UK police call off guard for Assange
Al Jazeera, Assange rape investigation dropped

assange-ecuador-embassy.why: Guard was lifted in October 2015, not February 2015 (the listed Wikipedia page has this wrong; news headlines dated 12-13 October 2015 agree). Added Sweden's 2019 reopening and final closure. Both rest on search-result headlines and dates; article bodies were not read.

fort-st-angelo-order-of-malta.story:
Fort St Angelo is a fortress at Birgu on Malta's Grand Harbour, part of which is used under a treaty by the Sovereign Military Order of Malta. The Order is a Catholic lay religious order that runs humanitarian work worldwide and traces its history to the Knights Hospitaller of about 1099. It has an unusual position. It has no territory of its own, yet it has diplomatic relations with more than 110 countries and is treated by many as a sovereign body in international law, though some legal scholars dispute that.

The fort explains the name. The knights rebuilt it from the 1530s to the 1560s and used it as their headquarters during the Great Siege of Malta in 1565. They lost the island to Napoleon's forces in 1798. The British garrisoned the fort from 1800 to 1979. After a first agreement in 1991, Malta and the Order signed a new treaty on 5 December 1998, ratified in 2001 under Chapter 429 of Maltese law.

The treaty lists what is given and what is kept. Malta grants a right of use of the upper part of the fort, including the Grand Master's House and the Chapel of St Anne, as a seat for coordinating the Order's humanitarian work. The Order's seat and archives are inviolable, which means officials may not enter or seize them. Its property is immune from search and confiscation, and its vehicles carry diplomatic plates. It pays no customs duty on goods for official use, and Malta must try to keep water and power flowing on the same terms as for embassies. The Order's own tribunals hear employment disputes with its foreign staff.

Malta keeps the rest. The site cannot be sold, and if the Order stops using it, it returns to Malta. The Maltese flag flies beside the Order's. Except where the treaty says otherwise, Maltese courts have full and exclusive authority and Maltese law applies. The Order may not grant asylum there, and it must hand over to Malta anyone wanted for an offence or for deportation or extradition.

The treaty runs for 99 years, and either side may give notice in the 50th or 75th year, with the ending taking effect five years after notice. The arrangement is in force. For anyone hoping to obtain territory from a state, this shows what a long-established body with diplomatic ties has obtained for one part of one building. It came with no ownership and with an exit date written into the text.
fort-st-angelo-order-of-malta.why: Added Article 15(2)(c) from the treaty text.

guantanamo-lease.story:
Guantánamo Bay is a US naval base on 117 square kilometres of land and water at the southeastern end of Cuba, held under a lease since 1903. It is the oldest American naval base overseas.

In 1901 the US Congress passed the Platt Amendment, which said Cuba would sell or lease land to the United States for coaling or naval stations, so that ships could refuel. The Cuban constitutional convention resisted at first, then wrote the amendment into the constitution that took effect in 1902. The lease followed in 1903.

The lease splits two ideas that usually go together. Article 3 says Cuba keeps "ultimate sovereignty", meaning the final legal title, while the United States exercises sole jurisdiction, meaning it alone makes and applies law there. The land may be used as a coaling and naval station only. Rent was $2,000 a year in gold until 1934, when the United States changed it to dollars, and since 1974 it has been $4,085 a year. A 1934 treaty says the lease can end only if both sides agree or the United States leaves the base. So the United States can hold on for as long as it chooses, simply by staying.

From 1953 to 1959 thousands of Cubans commuted to jobs on the base. After the revolution, the government that took power in 1959 began protesting that the base had been imposed by force and is illegal under international law. Cuba has cashed only one rent cheque since then, and Fidel Castro said that one was deposited by mistake. In late 1961 Cuban troops planted an 8-mile barrier of prickly pear cactus along the 17-mile fence, called the Cactus Curtain, to stop people crossing to the base.

Since 2002 the base has held a detention camp for people captured in the US war on terror. Because the final title lies with Cuba, a legal question arose as to whether US courts reached the base. In Boumediene v. Bush in 2008 the US Supreme Court ruled that detainees there have a constitutional right to challenge their detention in court. The split between title and control therefore did not put the base outside the US Constitution. Fifteen detainees remained in January 2025. That year the Trump administration also began sending undocumented migrants to the base. Lawsuits claim that those held lack access to lawyers and face harsh conditions, and a 2025 court ruling went against advocates seeking to stop the transfers.

The base still operates, and Cuba still objects. The holder here is a powerful government with a military base on the land, and the owner's objection since 1959 has not changed who controls it.

nasseri-charles-de-gaulle.story:
Mehran Karimi Nasseri was an Iranian man who lived in the departure lounge of Terminal 1 at Charles de Gaulle Airport near Paris from 26 August 1988 until July 2006, almost 18 years. Airports have a transit area, where travellers between international flights wait without passing immigration or customs, but such an area is fully under the law of the country where it sits. A person who breaks the law there can be prosecuted by that country.

Nasseri was born in 1945 in an oil company town in Iran and studied in Britain at the University of Bradford. He said he had been expelled from Iran in 1977 for protesting against the Shah, a claim later investigation disputed, and that after a long battle the UN refugee agency in Belgium gave him refugee status, which allowed him to live in other European countries. In 1988 he travelled towards Britain and his papers disappeared. He said they were stolen, and other accounts say he mailed them to Brussels from the ferry. Britain sent him back to France because he had no passport. At the French airport he could not prove who he was or what his status was, and he was detained in the waiting area.

Without papers he had no way to enter France. Lawyers argued over his status for years while he lived on a bench in the terminal. Belgium granted him residency in 1995 on condition that he live under supervision, and France granted residency in 1999. He then refused to sign the papers, because they listed him as Iranian and did not use the name he had chosen, "Sir, Alfred Mehran". So by the end the legal block had gone, and he stayed by his own decision.

He stayed until he was taken to hospital in 2006, then lived in Paris shelters for 16 years. He returned to the airport in September 2022 and died there of a heart attack two months later. His autobiography appeared in 2004, and his story inspired the 2004 film The Terminal.

He never claimed the terminal as a separate place, and nobody treated it as one. His stay gave him no separate legal status. It shows what happens to a person without papers in a place that belongs to a state and offers him no way in.

panama-canal-zone.story:
The Panama Canal Zone was a strip of 1,432 square kilometres across Panama that the United States governed from 1903 to 1979. It covered the canal and land about five miles either side of its centre line, and left out the cities of Panama City and Colón.

The United States wanted a canal so that its warships could move between oceans, a need made clear in the Spanish-American War of 1898, when warships in the Atlantic had to reach battles in the Pacific. A French firm had already failed at the job. Panama was then part of Colombia. When the Colombian Senate held out for better terms in 1903, President Theodore Roosevelt's government gave covert support to rebels in Panama and protected them when they declared independence that November. The treaty signed on 18 November by Philippe Bunau-Varilla, a Frenchman acting for the new republic, let the United States build the canal. The Isthmian Canal Convention proclaimed in 1904 gave it use, occupation and control of a zone in perpetuity, which means with no end date. The United States also bought out the land from its private and public owners.

The zone had its own governor, police, courts and judges, including a US district court, and its capital at Balboa, and US dollars as currency, with the Panamanian balboa tolerated. Almost everyone worked for the canal company or the government. Residents did not own their homes. They rented houses assigned mainly by seniority, and they bought goods at stores run by the company. The residents were known as Zonians.

The zone cut Panama in two, and that caused growing conflict, with rioting in 1958, 1959 and January 1964, after which Panamanian flags were allowed to fly beside American ones. Years of negotiation led to the Torrijos-Carter Treaties of 1977, which drew fierce controversy in the United States and passed the US Senate in March and April 1978 by 68 votes to 32 each time. The zone was abolished on 1 October 1979, and the canal itself was run jointly until it passed fully to Panama on 31 December 1999.

The grant in perpetuity therefore lasted 75 years. The legal text did not stop the two countries from replacing it by a further treaty, after decades of unrest over the zone.

add_sources.t: Torrijos-Carter Treaties

panama-canal-zone.why: The 23 percent poll figure was not found on the listed source or the Torrijos-Carter page. Replaced with the documented Senate votes.

snowden-sheremetyevo.story:
Edward Snowden, an American who leaked secret documents about US surveillance, spent 39 days in the transit area of Sheremetyevo Airport in Moscow in 2013. A transit area is the part of an airport where travellers wait between international flights without passing through immigration. It can look like a place outside any country, and it is not, as Russian law applied there the whole time.

The United States charged him under the Espionage Act of 1917 and with theft of government property, and asked Hong Kong to hold him. Hong Kong said the request did not fully meet its law and let him go. On 23 June he flew to Moscow with Sarah Harrison of WikiLeaks. WikiLeaks said he was heading for asylum in Ecuador, and he held an Ecuadorian emergency travel document.

He had a seat booked on an onward flight to Cuba, which he did not take. The State Department revoked his passport, and accounts differ on when and why this stranded him. Snowden said the United States wanted him to stay in Moscow so that it could call him a Russian spy. The journalist Glenn Greenwald said the passport was cancelled during the flight, so that he could not buy a ticket onward. The Russian newspaper Kommersant reported that Cuba had told Moscow it would not let the plane land, after American pressure.

Without a passport he could not board another flight, and he could not enter Russia without its agreement. President Vladimir Putin said he was in the transit area, had committed no crime in Russia and was free to leave. WikiLeaks announced that he had applied for asylum in several more countries. On 23 July the US Attorney General wrote to Russia's justice minister offering a limited passport good only for a direct return to the United States, and promising that Snowden would not face torture or the death penalty.

On 1 August 2013, after 39 days in the transit area, he left it with temporary asylum in Russia for one year. On 26 September 2022 Putin granted him Russian citizenship. He became president of the Freedom of the Press Foundation, a San Francisco nonprofit, in 2016.

An airport corridor gave him no independent standing. What he could do next was decided by Russian officials, by the American cancellation of his passport, and by the countries at the other end of each possible flight.
snowden-sheremetyevo.why: Exact length and date, and asylum was temporary at first.

un-headquarters-zones.story:
The United Nations runs its headquarters in New York and its offices in Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi as a kind of international concession, meaning an area inside a country where another body has been given some authority. Most local and national law still applies in them.

The arrangement exists for a practical reason. Delegates from every member country must be able to attend meetings, including those whose governments are on bad terms with the host. So the host country agrees on special entry rules. The United States has a special visa, the C-2, which lets foreign officials who would otherwise be barred enter the country, on condition that they stay near the headquarters.

Countries have made similar deals with each other. The Tomb of Suleyman Shah, grandfather of the founder of the Ottoman Empire, lies in northern Syria and was made a Turkish concession by the Treaty of Ankara in 1921. The tomb was moved in 1973 because the new Euphrates Lake would flood the site. In 2015 Turkey moved it again on its own because of the Syrian civil war. Syria called that move incompatible with the 1921 treaty, and in December 2017 Prime Minister Binali Yıldırım said the tomb would return to its second site, on the east bank of the Euphrates, once conditions allowed. No return is known to have taken place.

The Tangier International Zone in Morocco was a larger example, a concession of 373 square kilometres run by a group of foreign powers from 1923 to 1956, with its own legislative assembly. It ended when Morocco regained full sovereignty. Each of these rested on an agreement with the state whose land it was.

add_sources.t: Stockholm Center for Freedom, Süleyman Shah Tomb

un-headquarters-zones.why: Dated and attributed the statement on returning the tomb.

asgardia.story:
Asgardia is a self-declared space nation run from Vienna, Austria, whose only territory has been one small satellite. The Russian engineer Igor Ashurbeyli, who had founded a space research centre in Vienna in 2013, announced it at a press conference in Paris on 12 October 2016. The name comes from Asgard, the home of the gods in Norse myth.

The reason given for the project is a real feature of space law. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 requires governments to authorise and supervise everything their citizens and companies do in space. Asgardia's backers wanted access to space free of existing nations, and they reasoned that if they became a nation themselves, they could escape those restrictions. They said they would apply to the United Nations and aimed at a settlement on the Moon by 2043. Members were not expected to move into space.

People could join online. Over 100,000 applied within two days and 500,000 within three weeks, though tougher checks cut the figure to about 210,000 by June 2017. A constitution passed that month, with no formal way to vote against it, and made the state a kingdom with Ashurbeyli at its head, a 150-seat parliament and a court. It names a planned cryptocurrency called the Solar. Parliament met in Vienna, and Ashurbeyli was inaugurated at the Hofburg palace on 25 June 2018. He was re-elected with 93.17 percent in September 2022.

On 12 November 2017 an Antares rocket from Virginia launched a Cygnus cargo spacecraft to the International Space Station. After leaving the station, Cygnus released the satellite Asgardia-1, weighing 2.8 kilograms, into orbit on 6 December. Asgardia then called itself the first nation with all its territory in space. Legal scholars disagreed, for reasons that show how the law works. American companies launched the satellite on a NASA-funded mission, so the United States was the launching state and had to answer for it. Article VIII of the treaty keeps legal authority over a spacecraft with the country that registers it, and Article II bars anyone from claiming space. A satellite is therefore a piece of property under some country's law, and it gives its owners no territory.

The satellite burned up in the atmosphere on 12 September 2022, and no replacement has been reported. A press release from Asgardia reports a congress in Dubai on 30 October 2025 and claims over one million citizens. No state or UN body recognises it, and no one has ever lived there.

add_sources.t: Jonathan's Space Report No. 743

asgardia.why: Satellite was launched on 12 November and released on 6 December 2017. Wikipedia gives 12 November for both; the orbital catalogue report dates the release.

bigelow-aerospace.story:
Bigelow Aerospace was an American company in North Las Vegas, Nevada, that built inflatable modules for living in space. An inflatable module launches folded and expands in orbit, which makes it roomier and lighter than a rigid one. Robert Bigelow, who had made his money from the Budget Suites of America hotel chain, founded the company in 1998 and paid for it himself.

NASA had worked on the idea in a project called TransHab, which Congress cancelled in the late 1990s because of delays and budget limits. In 2000 Bigelow licensed the technology. It flew two uncrewed prototypes, Genesis I and II, in 2006 and 2007. In December 2012 NASA signed a $17.8 million contract for an expandable module called BEAM, which was added to the International Space Station in April 2016. By 2013 Bigelow had put in $250 million of his own money, and he said he would spend up to about $500 million. In 2010 it announced plans for a modular set of space habitats for creating or expanding stations.

Article VI of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty requires the United States to authorise and supervise its companies in space, and the company sought clear rules for private stations from regulators. In December 2014 the Federal Aviation Administration, which licenses rocket launches, reviewed a proposed Bigelow habitat on the Moon and wrote to Bigelow saying it could use its existing review of a launch's payload to cover such missions. Lawyers at the group TechFreedom criticised this as having no clear limits. A private habitat would therefore still need American permission.

In March 2020 Bigelow laid off all 88 staff and blamed the COVID-19 pandemic. When its engineering contract with NASA ended, NASA took ownership of BEAM in December 2021, and it has been cleared to stay on the station until 2031. The company was described as defunct as of January 2024. Nobody ever lived on its free-flying modules. The one module people could enter passed to a government agency.
bigelow-aerospace.why: FAA review concerned a lunar habitat. Added the BEAM transfer date and clearance to 2031.

flags-of-convenience-space.story:
A flag of convenience is a practice from shipping. Every merchant ship must be registered in a country and fly its flag, and that country's law then applies on board. Owners can choose to register in a country with light rules and low fees, even one the ship never visits. Lawyers have asked whether spacecraft can do the same, since a spacecraft also has a country of registry, under the UN Registration Convention and Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty.

The Registration Convention narrows the choice in a way shipping law does not. It says the country of registry must be a launching state, meaning one that launches the craft, arranges the launch, or provides the territory or facility it leaves from. Where several countries qualify, they agree among themselves which one registers it. So a company cannot simply pick any country's list as a shipowner can. Reading the text plainly, the chosen country must have some part in the launch.

Adrian Taghdiri wrote a 2013 note in the Boston University Journal of Science and Technology Law, as space tourism was starting, predicting that some countries would set loose rules to attract private space companies. He warned of environmental harm, more debris and danger to passengers. He also argued that some states might ignore the penalties the treaty places on them for their private actors.

Space law limits the effect without removing it. The registering country keeps legal authority over a spacecraft and its crew. But a launching state, meaning a country that launches a craft, pays for its launch, or lets its soil be used, stays liable for damage under Article VII. So a cheap registry could lighten the rules that a company lives under, but it cannot remove the responsibility of the country where the rocket went up.

A presentation at a symposium of the UN's space law subcommittee in Vienna in 2016 set out the shipping idea and asked how it fits space objects. The closest working example involves orbital slots, the positions assigned to satellites. Tonga, a small Pacific kingdom, has a company called Tongasat, whose business of holding slots has been described as in effect a flag of convenience for space. Later filings of the kind came from Gibraltar, Papua New Guinea and Bermuda.

The practice has not been tested in any court. Choosing a light-touch registry might reduce supervision, but it would not produce independence, because the treaty keeps some state's law attached to every registered craft.

add_sources.t: UN Registration Convention

flags-of-convenience-space.why: Omitted the key limit: Registration Convention Articles I and II allow only a launching state to register. Fixed a stray comma.

perseverance.story:
Perseverance is a car-sized NASA rover that landed in Jezero crater on Mars on 18 February 2021, at the point marked here. The crater was chosen because its ancient river delta may hold signs of past life. The rover has been driving and collecting rock and soil samples ever since, sealing them in tubes, and it has left some sealed tubes on the surface for a later mission to bring back. NASA paused its plan for that return in 2023 over its cost and turned to industry and its Jet Propulsion Laboratory for a cheaper design. In January 2026 Congress passed a NASA budget under which the return mission stayed cancelled, so no date exists for collecting the tubes.

The tubes raise a legal point that most landers do not. They sit on the ground, separate from the rover, perhaps for many years. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, says the registering country keeps legal authority over a spacecraft, and that ownership of objects "and of their component parts" is not affected by being in space or by returning to Earth. So the tubes remain American as they lie on Mars. Article VIII also says that such objects found elsewhere must be returned to the registering country.

The Martian rock inside the tubes is a harder question. Article II bars countries from claiming land on Mars, and the treaty does not say plainly whether a piece of rock removed from the ground can be owned. The United States and others in the Artemis Accords, a set of non-binding principles, say that extracting resources is not in itself a claim to territory. Luxembourg, following the United States, has passed a national law letting its companies own resources they take from space, and Japan has passed a space resources law as well. Russia argues that extraction creates no ownership and that one country's law cannot reach beyond its jurisdiction. A UN working group created in 2022 is drafting principles, and its unofficial draft of July 2025 still leaves in brackets the sentence saying that extraction is not in itself national appropriation, and it sets out no rule on who owns what is taken. A founder hoping to use local rock and ice could therefore rely on a home country's law that allows ownership, and other countries would remain free to reject it.

add_sources.t: The Register, Congress and Mars Sample Return
The Space Review, COPUOS and space resources
UN working group, draft principles, July 2025
SpaceNews, Japan passes space resources law

perseverance.why: Sample return outcome was out of date. The unsettled rock question now says who argues what and where the UN draft stands.

apollo-17.story:
Apollo 17 was the last crewed NASA landing on the Moon, in December 1972, in a valley called Taurus-Littrow on the southeastern rim of Mare Serenitatis. Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt, a geologist, drove about 35.7 kilometres in a Lunar Roving Vehicle and brought back 110.52 kilograms of samples. The descent stage of their lander Challenger, the rover and a science package remain in the valley, and no one has landed there since.

Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, says the registering country keeps legal authority over its spacecraft and that landing does not change who owns them. There is no time limit. So the United States still owns the car and the rest of the hardware.

The same treaty leaves the valley unowned. Article II bars claims to land on the Moon, and the crew's stay gave no rights. The treaty does not explain how a country that cannot own the Moon comes to own rock taken from it. Countries now answer it differently. The Artemis Accords say extracting resources is not in itself a claim to territory, and the United States and Luxembourg have laws letting their companies own what they take. Russia argues that extraction creates no ownership and that one country's law cannot reach beyond its jurisdiction. Draft principles from a UN working group, in their July 2025 form, set out no rule on who owns what is taken.

add_sources.t: The Space Review, COPUOS and space resources
UN working group, draft principles, July 2025

apollo-17.why: Open question now states who argues what.

apollo-11.story:
Apollo 11 was the NASA mission that put the first people on the Moon, at Tranquility Base, in July 1969. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed in the lunar module Eagle, and its lower half, the descent stage, still stands there with an American flag, instruments and their bootprints. The coordinates are NASA's, measured from images taken by its Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter.

The flag invites an obvious question. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, had taken effect two years before the landing. Article II bars any country from claiming the Moon by any means, so the flag gave the United States no title. The ground under it stays unclaimed.

Article VIII says the country that registers a spacecraft keeps legal authority over it and that landing does not change who owns it. That covers the hardware only. So the descent stage and flag are American property. The bootprints are marks on ground nobody owns, and that rule does not cover them.

This gap has led to efforts to protect the site. The group For All Moonkind argues that places like Tranquility Base are human heritage. It helped draft the US One Small Step to Protect Human Heritage in Space Act, to turn NASA's preservation recommendations for Apollo sites into law. The Senate passed it unanimously in 2019, the House passed it in December 2020, and it became law on 31 December 2020. A national law of that kind reaches only those under US authority, and the treaty has no specific rule on heritage sites. The Artemis Accords, a non-binding set of principles, include an agreement to preserve historic landing sites and artifacts.
apollo-11.why: The Act became law; the text stopped at Senate passage. Added the Accords' heritage clause. The source page also gives 2021 once, which is inconsistent with House passage in December 2020.

artemis-accords.story:
The Artemis Accords are a set of non-binding principles for civil activity on the Moon and beyond, drawn up by NASA and the US State Department to go with NASA's Artemis program of Moon missions. Non-binding means no country can be taken to court for breaking them. Eight countries signed on 13 October 2020: Australia, Canada, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom and the United States. According to NASA, Vietnam became the 78th signatory on 28 October 2026.

The background is a gap in the law. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 bars countries from claiming land in space, and it guarantees free access to all areas. It also tells them to avoid harmful interference with one another. It does not say what happens when two missions want the same crater with ice in it. The Moon Agreement of 1979 tried to fill the gap by calling the Moon's resources the common heritage of humanity, to be managed under an international system. Only 18 countries ever joined.

The most debated part of the Accords is the safety zone. Signatories say they will announce where they are working and coordinate so that they do not interfere with each other. A zone covers an area where other operations could cause harmful interference. Its size and length depend on the work done there, and it ends when the work stops. Inside it, signatories say they still respect free access by others. NASA says this respects the treaty. The open question is how far a zone can go before it becomes the kind of claim the treaty forbids.

The Accords also say that extracting resources in space is possible before any further international rules exist, and that this is not in itself a claim to territory. A McGill University paper reads this as differing from the Moon Agreement, which calls for an international system first. Saudi Arabia signed the Accords in July 2022 and notified its withdrawal from the Moon Agreement six months later, which leaves 17 members. Russia called the Accords a blatant attempt to create international space law that favours the United States, and Chinese government-affiliated media compared them to European colonial land-taking. Frans von der Dunk of the University of Nebraska-Lincoln argues that they strengthen the American reading of the treaty, which allows commercial activity. The China-Russia lunar base project has been described as a rival.

No court has tested the zones. For a would-be founder, they show the most that current practice offers, which is a temporary priority at a place through use and notice, under a government's sponsorship, with no ownership. It lasts only as long as the work goes on.
artemis-accords.why: Moon Agreement count now current. Attributed the positions on the Accords.

fcc-starlink-licensing.story:
Outer space belongs to no country, yet a national telecoms regulator can set rules for what happens there. To see why, start with what a satellite needs. It must send radio signals to the ground, and to sell a service it must have customers on the ground. Radio frequencies are licensed by governments, working within the international system run by the International Telecommunication Union. So a regulator that controls access to customers has a hold over the satellite, even though the satellite itself sits in a place no country may claim.

The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) decides who may use radio frequencies to reach customers in the United States. In a 2018 order it allowed SpaceX to run a system of 4,425 satellites offering broadband internet around the world, under its Starlink plan. Under Article VI of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the United States must authorise and supervise its companies in space, and in practice the FCC does much of this for SpaceX.

The FCC has also shown that it can punish a company for what it leaves in orbit. In 2002 Dish Network launched a satellite called EchoStar-7 into geostationary orbit, the band 36,000 kilometres up where a satellite appears to hang over one spot on Earth. In 2012 Dish agreed to move it 186 miles higher at the end of its life, into a graveyard orbit out of the way of working satellites. In February 2022, low on fuel, it managed only about 76 miles. On 2 October 2023 the FCC announced its first fine for space debris. Dish admitted liability, paid $150,000 and accepted a compliance plan. The enforcement chief called this a breakthrough settlement showing the agency's strong authority.

A company that wants customers on the ground stays within reach of the regulator that licenses its signals. Anyone planning a separate community in orbit would meet the same regulator when trying to send signals to people on Earth or sell to them. Starlink's own 2020 beta terms made California law govern service on Earth and the Moon.

zuzalu.story:
Zuzalu was a temporary community of about 200 people at Lustica Bay, a resort on the Adriatic coast of Montenegro. It was conceived by Vitalik Buterin, a co-founder of the Ethereum cryptocurrency network, and ran for about two months from 25 March 2023. It set the model for later pop-up cities, in which people who met online live in one place for weeks or months.

Participants came from crypto, drug companies, politics and universities. They stayed mostly in resort hotels and rented homes, with the five-star Chedi Lustica Bay as the main base. Topics included cryptocurrency, artificial intelligence and the science of longer life, and the longevity group VitaDAO helped organise a three-day science conference. A main theme of that track was finding a new jurisdiction and set of rules for longevity medicine.

Another topic was the network state, an idea from the former Coinbase executive Balaji Srinivasan in which an online community eventually buys land and seeks its own laws. Srinivasan appeared by video. The news site Decrypt reported that some compared the event to Burning Man for futurists and others to a sleepaway camp for the crypto elite.

Daily life was loosely organised. Talks and seminars were arranged by participants, breakfast was served every day at a local restaurant taken over for the event, and a philosophy group met in the hotel sauna until the management asked it to stop. One group handed out worthless Venezuelan bolivar notes as party invitations, then built an app that used the serial numbers as a test identity system. The writer Jonathan Hillis later called the location too expensive and inconvenient, and said it had produced no longer-term plan for a permanent base.

No land was taken and no new law was reported. Everyone remained under Montenegrin law and went home when the two months were over. Later projects, including Vitalia and Zuitzerland, grew out of it. It tested how a community organises itself and asked nothing of the host country's law.

blue-ghost-1.story:
Blue Ghost Mission 1 was a robotic Moon landing by Firefly Aerospace, an American private company, on a NASA-backed flight carrying ten experiments. It landed in Mare Crisium, near Mons Latreille, on 2 March 2025, and it is described as the first fully successful soft landing by a commercial company. It worked until the batteries ran down after sunset on 16 March.

Because the lander belongs to a company, it shows how the law treats private hardware. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, addresses private companies directly. Article VI makes the United States responsible for authorising and supervising its companies in space, and makes it answerable for what they do. Article VIII protects the company's ownership of the machine and leaves legal authority with the country that registered it.

The company gains no land. Article II bars national claims to the Moon. So a private lander is private property under a government's supervision, standing on ground nobody owns.

mars-society-city-state.story:
The Mars Society is an American volunteer nonprofit, funded by donations, that lobbies for human missions to Mars. The engineer Robert Zubrin founded it on 13 August 1998 at a convention of 750 people in Boulder, Colorado.

All its physical work has been on Earth. It runs analogue stations, meaning simulated Mars bases, on Devon Island in the Canadian Arctic and in the desert at its Mars Desert Research Station. Crews live there under mission rules for weeks or months, including an 80-day stay in 2017.

It has also asked how a society on Mars would be organised. In 2019 it held a contest to design a colony of 1,000, won by a Massachusetts Institute of Technology team with a plan called Star City, made up of five starting villages. In 2020 it announced a second contest for a city state of one million people, with a $10,000 prize. A city state is a single city that rules itself as a country. Zubrin's 2024 book The New World on Mars predicts populous Martian city-states with governments of the people that draw immigrants from Earth, paying for imports through enterprises such as real estate.

These designs have no legal force, and the society has adopted no known constitution for Mars. The law as it stands points in another direction. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars any country from claiming land there, and it makes each country responsible for its citizens' activities in space. So a settlement on Mars would begin as an activity supervised by some country on Earth. How such a settlement could move to self-rule under the treaty has not been settled.
